Dynamic Resonator by NeutronStar714: a four-band audio effect that turns input dynamics into filter-frequency movement.
Built with C++ and JUCE. Available as VST3 and standalone, version 1.3.0.
Let the sound move the filter.
A four-band effect that translates changes in input loudness into moving filter frequencies. Each band can follow the envelope upward or downward, with its own sensitivity.
Move the envelope slider, then change a band’s direction or sensitivity.
Visual demonstration of the plugin’s frequency mapping. The envelope is set manually here; in the plugin, it follows incoming audio. No audio is processed on this page.

Instead of keeping the filter frequencies fixed, Dynamic Resonator uses the incoming signal’s envelope as a control source. A louder passage can push one band upward while pulling another downward. Sensitivity determines how far each band travels.
The movement is logarithmic: the controls work across octaves, connecting small changes in the envelope to a broad frequency sweep. Setting a band’s sensitivity to zero keeps its frequency fixed.
Attack and release set how quickly the envelope responds. RMS and AM detection offer different ways of following the input.
The dynamic-range window maps a chosen span of envelope levels to the full modulation range. Levels below it hold the starting position; levels above it reach maximum movement.
The plugin interface combines a filter-response display with input and processed spectra, plus meters for the raw and mapped envelopes.
The envelope follower listens after pre-gain and controls each filter’s frequency. The original input remains available through the dry path.
C++17 and JUCE; stereo IIR filters.
20 Hz–20 kHz base frequency; Q from 0.1 to 10 for each band.
2,048-point FFT with a Hann window for the input and wet spectra.
Plugin parameters are saved and restored with the host session.
About NeutronStar714 — a chemistry and music technology applicant who composes electronic music, builds VST3 audio plugins in C++ and JUCE, plays in the school band G10, and photographs.
I am a high-school student who composes, produces, programs and photographs. I am applying to study chemistry and music technology.

Chemistry is my primary academic subject. Music technology is the second thing I want to study, and it is the half of my work that can be shown rather than described — finished releases, running software, and images.

Most of what is on this site I made on my own: the electronic releases are written, performed, mixed and produced by me, and the plugins are programmed by me in C++ with JUCE. The rock songs are the exception, because those are a band effort.
I began composing in GarageBand at eleven, improvising on a MIDI keyboard and learning the software as I went. My first album,
, came out of that period in December 2020.
, the following year, was the first album I made in FL Studio.
Each album since has been a deliberate step.
(2023) was written while I was teaching myself mixing and sound design.
(2024) is where the sound I call Resonance Electronica is clearest — synth plucks layered with filter envelopes and resonances, under heavy distortion.
was my first attempt at house music, and
(2025) is a double album that leaves distortion behind on disc one and returns to the retro style on disc two.
collection gathers unreleased singles and B-sides from 2020 to 2024, among them “The Universe” and “π”, which I wrote with a friend who was as interested in science as I was.
G10 is my school band. Together we have written and recorded two original songs, which I recorded, mixed and produced with my bandmates.
I build my own audio software. The four plugins I have finished are VST3 effects written in C++ with JUCE, and each one begins with an idea of my own rather than a recreation of a classic effect.

Dynamic Resonator, the first to be written up for this site, is a four-band effect that reads the envelope of the incoming signal and moves each filter's frequency in response — upward or downward, at a sensitivity set per band, with its own attack and release.

Photography is the newest of the four. I photograph hiking trips, highways and cities, and the interest is compositional rather than documentary: I am after images that say something about a place, not only images that record it.

The album where all distortion is suddenly gone, and the audience is greet with clear and soft synthesizer sounds. I experimented with many minimalist composing techniques, introducing variations with addition of elements many automations instead of using a verse-chorous-verse structure. Disc 1 of this album is also considered as my turning-away from adopting solely my personal style, instead, it included many elements from comtemporary electronic music. Disc 2 is a continuation of my former style, the "retro", best represented by "Plumbium".
Created Someone Else's Work I Guess.

As the cover shows, Earlier is a collection of unreleased singles, edits, or "B-sides" from 2020 to 2024. The first six songs except for "Oh." are my absolute earilest works composed using Garageband and mostly improvisation on a MIDI keyboard. They mark some of my happiest memories in the transition from a child to a teenager; among them, "The Universe" and "π" stands out, which I created together with a friend who, just like me, were keen in science across many disciplines. Later in the list, songs 7~9 are the products of a transition period embedded in the making of Expression and Emotion when I kinda got lost in which direction to develope my musical style, and songs 10~11 are unreleased B-sides between Expression and Emotion and Resonance from the Distance.
Maybe the closest call for me to approach the mainstream music genres. My first trial of making house music, blending my own musical elements into energetic drum machine loops and basslines.

The massive use of distortion on almost every synthesizer, instrument, and samples used characterize of this album. At the same time, my very own musical genre "Resonance Electronica" is most overtly manifested in this album. Layering synth plucks with filter envelopes and resonance, an almost iconic sound effect is created and used throughout the album.

Definitely an emotional outlet for my 13-year-old self. I may be a late boomer to many, and at the time, little to no thought exchange with peers since there's no one to share them with. Thoughts specified by the names of some of those songs are preserved, and emotion was expressed with this album. The music lies in a transition, for I kept on fumbling the mixing and sound designing techniques in FL Studio by myself, but not actually manged to apply them well. It's definitely smoother than 2048, but not as delicate as Resonance from the Distance.

The three songs are the products of experimenting wildly with newly gained knowledge in FL Studio, in which only "Sense" was selected to be included in the next album. "Electrical Experiment" and "Actuallized" may be viewed as naive and irregular uses of effects, which made them not as pleasant to listen to.

The first album made with FL Studio, and of course, with not much knowledge and techniques in mixing and sound design. Starting off with little idea of using such a powerful tool, I focused more on the music itself rather than polishing my mixing. The album is represented by its stark yet complicated 16th drum patterns, my "iconic" Ogun riff, and the occasional use of microtonal pitch shifts.
A Drive into Town Blade for AA12

The name of this album is set by a 11-year-old me not yet proficient in English ("want" is the same meaning to that in "wanted"), it's alternate title "Neon Light Stray" may better display the meaning of this album, in which I pictured a very unlucky poor man living a vagrant life in a metropolitan city. The use of soft and dreamy synthesizers from Garageband constructed this particular atmostphere, best represented in UnsubscribeToDream #5.
